topic: Agency Disclosure and Duties to Parties
question: Under MREC Administrative Rule 4.1 (Agency Relationship Disclosure), the purpose of the agency disclosure rule is to ensure consumers are fully informed of the agency relationships identified in which section of Mississippi law?
choice_a: Miss. Code Ann. Section 89-1-501
choice_b: Miss. Code Ann. Section 73-35-21
choice_c: Miss. Code Ann. Section 73-35-11
choice_d: Miss. Code Ann. Section 73-35-3
explanation: MREC Rule 4.1 states that consumers shall be fully informed of the agency relationships in real estate transactions identified in Section 73-35-3 (which defines 'real estate broker,' 'brokerage agreement,' and related terms). The rule also clarifies that it does not abrogate the common law of agency, and compliance protects licensees from Commission sanctions but does not automatically satisfy every common-law fiduciary duty.
source_note: MREC Rules and Regulations, Part 1601, Ch. 4, Rule 4.1 (source: Miss. Code Ann. Section 73-35-3)

topic: Agency Disclosure and Duties to Parties
question: In a single agency relationship, when must a Mississippi broker disclose in writing, on the MREC Agency Disclosure Form, that the broker is the agent of the party the broker represents?
choice_a: Before the time an agreement for representation is entered into between the broker and that party
choice_b: Within ten days after closing
choice_c: At the first substantive meeting only if the party requests it
choice_d: Only if the transaction involves dual compensation
explanation: MREC Rule 4.3(A) requires that in a single agency, the broker disclose in writing to the party the broker represents that the broker is that party's agent, and this written disclosure must be made before the time an agreement for representation (e.g., a listing or buyer representation agreement) is entered into, on the MREC Agency Disclosure Form.
source_note: MREC Rules and Regulations, Part 1601, Ch. 4, Rule 4.3(A)

topic: Agency Disclosure and Duties to Parties
question: In a single agency transaction, a Mississippi broker representing the seller must disclose in writing to a buyer who is NOT represented by that broker that the broker is the agent of another party. When must this disclosure occur?
choice_a: Before the property is listed
choice_b: At the time of the first substantive meeting with the unrepresented party
choice_c: At closing
choice_d: Only upon written request from the unrepresented party
explanation: MREC Rule 4.3(B) requires that, in a single agency, the broker disclose in writing to the party for whom the broker is not an agent that the broker represents another party in the transaction, and this disclosure must be made at the time of the 'first substantive meeting' with that unrepresented party, using the MREC Agency Disclosure Form.
source_note: MREC Rules and Regulations, Part 1601, Ch. 4, Rule 4.3(B)

topic: Agency Disclosure and Duties to Parties
question: The Mississippi Real Estate Commission's mandated agency disclosure form may be reproduced by licensees, but what restriction applies to that reproduction under Rule 4.3(G)?
choice_a: It may only be reproduced in color
choice_b: It must be re-notarized each time it is copied
choice_c: It may be duplicated in content and size, but it may not be altered
choice_d: It may only be used once per calendar year
explanation: Rule 4.3(G) provides that the Commission-mandated disclosure form 'may be duplicated in content and size but not altered.' Licensees may reproduce the form (for example, on letterhead) but cannot change its substantive language or required content.
source_note: MREC Rules and Regulations, Part 1601, Ch. 4, Rule 4.3(G)

topic: Agency Disclosure and Duties to Parties
question: Under MREC Rule 4.2(H), for a broker acting as the SELLER's agent, the 'first substantive meeting' triggering mandatory disclosure occurs before or immediately prior to which of the following?
choice_a: The buyer's mortgage pre-approval
choice_b: The closing of the transaction
choice_c: The listing agreement's expiration date
choice_d: Showing the property to a prospective buyer, eliciting confidential buyer information, or executing an agreement governed by Section 73-35-3
explanation: Rule 4.2(H)(1) defines 'first substantive meeting' for a seller's agent as occurring before or just immediately prior to the first of: showing the property to a prospective buyer, eliciting confidential information from a buyer about the buyer's needs, motivation, or financial qualifications, or the execution of any agreement governed by Section 73-35-3.
source_note: MREC Rules and Regulations, Part 1601, Ch. 4, Rule 4.2(H)(1)

topic: Agency Disclosure and Duties to Parties
question: Which of the following is expressly EXCLUDED from triggering the seller's agent's 'first substantive meeting' disclosure obligation under MREC Rule 4.2(H)(2)?
choice_a: A bona fide open house or model home showing (absent eliciting confidential information or executing an agreement)
choice_b: Eliciting a buyer's confidential financial qualifications
choice_c: Executing a purchase agreement with the buyer
choice_d: Signing a buyer representation agreement
explanation: Rule 4.2(H)(2) excludes a bona fide 'open house' or model home showing from triggering the first substantive meeting definition, along with preliminary 'small talk' about price range, location, and property styles, and responding to general factual questions about advertised properties -- unless confidential information is elicited or an agreement is executed during that event.
source_note: MREC Rules and Regulations, Part 1601, Ch. 4, Rule 4.2(H)(2)

topic: Agency Disclosure and Duties to Parties
question: A prospective buyer asks a listing agent at an open house general factual questions about the advertised list price and square footage of the home. Under MREC Rule 4.2(H)(2)(c), does this conversation, by itself, trigger the agency disclosure obligation?
choice_a: Yes, any conversation with a prospective buyer triggers disclosure
choice_b: No, responding to general factual questions about advertised properties is excluded from the first substantive meeting definition
choice_c: Yes, but only if the buyer later makes an offer
choice_d: It depends solely on whether the buyer is pre-approved for financing
explanation: Rule 4.2(H)(2)(c) specifically excludes 'responding to general factual questions from a prospective buyer concerning properties that have been advertised for sale or lease' from the definition of first substantive meeting, so this exchange alone does not require agency disclosure.
source_note: MREC Rules and Regulations, Part 1601, Ch. 4, Rule 4.2(H)(2)(c)

topic: Agency Disclosure and Duties to Parties
question: For a broker representing a BUYER, MREC Rule 4.2(H)(3) defines the 'first substantive meeting' as occurring at the initial contact with a seller or seller's agent, or before or immediately prior to which additional events?
choice_a: The buyer's loan application only
choice_b: The buyer's home inspection
choice_c: Showing the seller's property to the represented buyer, eliciting confidential information from the seller, or executing an agreement governed by Section 73-35-3
choice_d: The recording of the deed
explanation: Rule 4.2(H)(3) mirrors the seller's-agent definition for a buyer's agent: first substantive meeting occurs at initial contact with a seller or seller's agent, or before/immediately prior to showing the seller's property to the represented buyer, eliciting confidential information from the seller, or the execution of an agreement governed by Section 73-35-3.
source_note: MREC Rules and Regulations, Part 1601, Ch. 4, Rule 4.2(H)(3)

topic: Agency Disclosure and Duties to Parties
question: Under MREC Rule 4.3(D), if a party to a real estate transaction is not available to sign an agency disclosure form, how may the broker satisfy the disclosure requirement?
choice_a: The broker may skip disclosure entirely for that party
choice_b: The broker must postpone the transaction until the party is available
choice_c: The broker must have another licensee sign on the party's behalf
choice_d: The disclosure may be accomplished orally, with the broker noting this on the form and forwarding it for signature as soon as possible; written electronic transmission also satisfies the requirement
explanation: Rule 4.3(D) permits oral disclosure when a party is unavailable to sign, provided the broker annotates the applicable form and forwards it for signature as soon as possible; the rule also confirms that written electronic transmission fulfills the disclosure requirement.
source_note: MREC Rules and Regulations, Part 1601, Ch. 4, Rule 4.3(D)

topic: Agency Disclosure and Duties to Parties
question: If a party receiving an agency disclosure form refuses to sign it to acknowledge receipt, what must the broker do under MREC Rule 4.3(E)?
choice_a: Annotate the form with a statement that a copy was delivered on a stated date and the recipient declined to acknowledge receipt
choice_b: Void the transaction immediately
choice_c: Report the refusal to the Attorney General
choice_d: Nothing further is required
explanation: Rule 4.3(E) requires the broker to annotate the disclosure form with the prescribed statement: 'A COPY OF THIS FORM WAS DELIVERED TO ___ DATE ___. RECIPIENT DECLINED TO ACKNOWLEDGE RECEIPT OF THIS FORM.' This protects the broker's compliance record even without the party's signature.
source_note: MREC Rules and Regulations, Part 1601, Ch. 4, Rule 4.3(E)

topic: Agency Disclosure and Duties to Parties
question: MREC Rule 4.2(F) defines a 'Disclosed Dual Agent' as a broker representing both parties to a transaction under what condition?
choice_a: Only if the broker waives all compensation
choice_b: With the informed consent of both parties and a written understanding of the specific duties and representation afforded each party
choice_c: Automatically whenever a broker lists and sells the same property
choice_d: Only with oral consent
explanation: Rule 4.2(F) defines a Disclosed Dual Agent as one representing both parties to a real estate transaction with the informed consent of both parties, accompanied by a written understanding of the specific duties and representation to be afforded each party -- consent must be informed and documented, not automatic or merely oral.
source_note: MREC Rules and Regulations, Part 1601, Ch. 4, Rule 4.2(F)

topic: Agency Disclosure and Duties to Parties
question: A Mississippi broker seeks to act as a disclosed dual agent representing both the buyer and seller. Under MREC Rule 4.3(B), when must the broker obtain the informed written consent of all parties?
choice_a: At closing only
choice_b: Only after the offer is accepted
choice_c: Prior to or at the time of formalization of the dual agency
choice_d: Consent is not required if both parties are represented by the same salesperson
explanation: Rule 4.3(B) requires brokers operating as disclosed dual agents to obtain informed written consent of all parties 'prior to or at the time of formalization of the dual agency,' with specific mechanisms (MREC Form A and the Dual Agency Confirmation Form) prescribed for timely compliance.
source_note: MREC Rules and Regulations, Part 1601, Ch. 4, Rule 4.3(B)

topic: Agency Disclosure and Duties to Parties
question: Under MREC Rule 4.3(B)(1), when must a SELLER give written consent to disclosed dual agency by signing the Consent to Dual Agency portion of MREC Form A?
choice_a: Only after the property has an accepted offer
choice_b: At the final walkthrough
choice_c: Within 30 days after closing
choice_d: At the time an agreement for representation is entered into between the broker and the seller
explanation: Rule 4.3(B)(1) specifies that the seller gives written consent to dual agency at the time an agreement for representation (i.e., the listing agreement) is entered into between the broker and the seller, by signing the Consent to Dual Agency portion of MREC Form A.
source_note: MREC Rules and Regulations, Part 1601, Ch. 4, Rule 4.3(B)(1)

topic: Agency Disclosure and Duties to Parties
question: Under MREC Rule 4.3(B)(3), before a buyer signs an offer to purchase in a disclosed dual agency transaction, what must the broker confirm and document?
choice_a: That the buyer understands and consents to the dual agency, evidenced by the buyer signing the MREC Dual Agency Confirmation Form attached to the offer to purchase
choice_b: That the buyer has obtained a home inspection
choice_c: That the buyer has hired independent legal counsel
choice_d: That the seller has reduced the listing price
explanation: Rule 4.3(B)(3) requires the broker to confirm that the buyer understands and consents to the consensual dual agency relationship prior to the buyer signing an offer to purchase, with the buyer's consent evidenced by signing the MREC Dual Agency Confirmation Form, which is then attached to the offer to purchase.
source_note: MREC Rules and Regulations, Part 1601, Ch. 4, Rule 4.3(B)(3)

topic: Agency Disclosure and Duties to Parties
question: In a disclosed dual agency, the seller must also confirm consent before the broker presents the buyer's offer to purchase. Under MREC Rule 4.3(B)(3), does the Dual Agency Confirmation Form remain attached to the offer if the offer is ultimately rejected?
choice_a: No, it is discarded once the offer is rejected
choice_b: Yes, the form shall remain attached to the offer to purchase regardless of the outcome of the offer
choice_c: Only if the rejection is in writing
choice_d: Only if the Commission requests it
explanation: Rule 4.3(B)(3) expressly states that the seller's signed Dual Agency Confirmation Form 'shall remain attached to the offer to purchase regardless of the outcome of the offer to purchase,' preserving a documented consent trail for the transaction file irrespective of whether the offer is accepted or rejected.
source_note: MREC Rules and Regulations, Part 1601, Ch. 4, Rule 4.3(B)(3)

topic: Agency Disclosure and Duties to Parties
question: MREC Rule 4.1 cautions brokers practicing disclosed dual agency to exercise the utmost caution because of what risk?
choice_a: Increased continuing education requirements
choice_b: Higher errors and omissions insurance premiums in all cases
choice_c: Situations may arise where disclosed dual agency presents conflicts of interest that cannot be resolved without breaching a duty to one party or the other
choice_d: A mandatory reduction in commission
explanation: Rule 4.1 (read with Rule 4.2(F)) warns that 'there may be situations where disclosed dual agency presents conflicts of interest that cannot be resolved without breach of duty to one party or another,' and directs brokers practicing disclosed dual agency to proceed with the utmost caution to protect both consumers and themselves.
source_note: MREC Rules and Regulations, Part 1601, Ch. 4, Rule 4.2(F) and Rule 4.1

topic: Agency Disclosure and Duties to Parties
question: Miss. Code Ann. Section 73-35-21(1)(e) lists which act as grounds for the Real Estate Commission to refuse, suspend, or revoke a license?
choice_a: Advertising a property with a 'for sale' sign
choice_b: Charging a commission above a set percentage
choice_c: Requiring a written brokerage agreement before showing a home
choice_d: Acting for more than one party in a transaction, or receiving compensation from more than one party in a transaction, or both, without the knowledge of all parties for whom the licensee acts
explanation: Section 73-35-21(1)(e) is Mississippi's core statutory prohibition against undisclosed dual agency and undisclosed dual compensation: a licensee who acts for more than one party, or accepts compensation from more than one party, without the knowledge of all parties represented, is subject to license discipline. This statute is the backbone that MREC's Rule 4 disclosure and consent procedures are designed to satisfy.
source_note: Miss. Code Ann. Section 73-35-21(1)(e)

topic: Agency Disclosure and Duties to Parties
question: If the agency relationship between the parties to a real estate transaction changes after the initial disclosure (for example, a single agency relationship becomes a dual agency), what does MREC Rule 4.3(C) require?
choice_a: New disclosure forms must be acknowledged by all parties involved
choice_b: No further action is required if the original disclosure form is still on file
choice_c: The Commission must approve the change before it takes effect
choice_d: Only the broker's initials are needed on the original form
explanation: Rule 4.3(C) provides that 'in the event the agency relationship changes between the parties to a real estate transaction, new disclosure forms will be acknowledged by all parties involved,' ensuring the written record always matches the current, actual agency relationship.
source_note: MREC Rules and Regulations, Part 1601, Ch. 4, Rule 4.3(C)

topic: Agency Disclosure and Duties to Parties
question: Under MREC Rule 4.2(D), how does 'compensation' relate to the existence of an agency relationship?
choice_a: Only the party who pays the commission can be the broker's client
choice_b: Compensation, standing alone, is not the determining factor -- an agency relationship can exist regardless of whether the seller, the buyer, both, or neither pays the fee
choice_c: Dual agency exists automatically whenever both parties contribute to the commission
choice_d: A broker cannot represent a party who pays no fee
explanation: Rule 4.2(D) states that compensation, considered alone, is NOT the determining factor in an agency relationship -- 'the relationship can be created regardless of whether the seller pays the fee, the buyer pays the fee, both pay the fee or neither pays a fee.' Who pays the commission does not by itself establish or negate who the broker's client is.
source_note: MREC Rules and Regulations, Part 1601, Ch. 4, Rule 4.2(D)

topic: Agency Disclosure and Duties to Parties
question: Under MREC Rule 4.2(B), a real estate broker is the agent of the principal (client) to whom a fiduciary obligation is owed. How does the rule characterize salespersons licensed under that broker?
choice_a: As independent brokers within the firm
choice_b: As co-clients with the broker
choice_c: As subagents of the broker, regardless of the location of the office in which the salesperson works
choice_d: As customers of the broker
explanation: Rule 4.2(B) is explicit that 'salespersons licensed under the broker are subagents of the Broker, regardless of the location of the office in which the salesperson works.' The broker -- not the individual salesperson -- is the true agent bearing the fiduciary obligation to the client.
source_note: MREC Rules and Regulations, Part 1601, Ch. 4, Rule 4.2(B)

topic: Agency Disclosure and Duties to Parties
question: Two salespersons who both work under the same responsible broker each separately represent the buyer and the seller in the same transaction, working out of the same or even different branch offices. Given MREC Rule 4.2(B)'s subagency structure, what is the legal effect for the firm?
choice_a: Each salesperson independently represents only their own party, with no dual agency implications for the firm
choice_b: This automatically voids the transaction under Mississippi law
choice_c: The salespersons, not the broker, bear the fiduciary duty in this scenario
choice_d: Because both salespersons are subagents of the same broker regardless of office location, the broker itself is deemed to represent both parties, creating a dual agency requiring disclosed consent
explanation: Because Rule 4.2(B) makes all salespersons subagents of the SAME broker regardless of branch office, both salespersons' representation flows up to and through the one responsible broker. The broker therefore is deemed to represent both parties, which constitutes dual agency requiring the informed written consent procedures under Rule 4.3(B) -- Mississippi's rule text does not carve out a 'designated agency' exception based on which salesperson or branch office is involved.
source_note: MREC Rules and Regulations, Part 1601, Ch. 4, Rule 4.2(B) and Rule 4.3(B)

topic: Agency Disclosure and Duties to Parties
question: Does the text of the Mississippi Real Estate Commission's agency disclosure rule provide for a 'designated agency' (sometimes called 'appointed agency') exception that would allow two salespersons within the same brokerage to each act as the sole agent of one party without triggering the firm's dual agency requirements?
choice_a: No -- Rule 4.2(B) instead makes every salesperson a subagent of the one responsible broker 'regardless of the location of the office,' so intra-firm representation of opposing parties is treated as dual agency of the broker, not designated agency
choice_b: Yes, designated agency is expressly authorized by Rule 4.2
choice_c: Yes, but only for transactions over a certain dollar threshold
choice_d: No, because Mississippi does not permit any form of dual agency
explanation: Mississippi's MREC Rule 4.2(B) text does not create a designated (appointed) agency exception. Instead, because every salesperson is defined as a subagent of the single responsible broker regardless of office location, having two salespersons at the same firm each work with an opposing party is handled under the disclosed dual agency framework in Rule 4.3(B), not as separate single agencies for each salesperson. This is distinct from choice D -- Mississippi does affirmatively permit disclosed dual agency, it just does not treat it as 'designated agency.'
source_note: MREC Rules and Regulations, Part 1601, Ch. 4, Rule 4.2(B)

topic: Agency Disclosure and Duties to Parties
question: Under MREC Rule 4.2(I), 'Single Agency' means a broker who has chosen to represent only one party to a transaction. Which of the following parties can that single represented party be, per the rule's text?
choice_a: Only the buyer
choice_b: The buyer, seller, lessor, lessee, or any party in a transaction governed by Section 73-35-3
choice_c: Only the seller
choice_d: Only institutional lenders
explanation: Rule 4.2(I) defines Single Agency broadly: 'a broker who has chosen to represent only one party to a real estate transaction. It may be either the buyer, seller, lessor or lessee or any party in a transaction governed by Section 73-35-3.'
source_note: MREC Rules and Regulations, Part 1601, Ch. 4, Rule 4.2(I)

topic: Agency Disclosure and Duties to Parties
question: A broker representing the seller has a salesperson who works with an unrepresented buyer in the same transaction. Because that salesperson is a subagent of the seller's broker under Rule 4.2(B), what disclosure obligation still applies to the unrepresented buyer?
choice_a: None, because the buyer is unrepresented
choice_b: Disclosure is required only if the buyer asks
choice_c: The salesperson must disclose in writing, at the first substantive meeting, that the broker (through the salesperson) represents another party (the seller)
choice_d: Disclosure may wait until the closing table
explanation: Even though the salesperson is only a subagent, the disclosure obligations under Rule 4.3(B) run through the broker's representation. The buyer, as the unrepresented 'customer' in a single agency, must still receive written disclosure at the first substantive meeting that the broker (whose subagent is working with the buyer) represents another party -- the seller.
source_note: MREC Rules and Regulations, Part 1601, Ch. 4, Rule 4.2(B) and Rule 4.3(B)

topic: Agency Disclosure and Duties to Parties
question: Under MREC Rule 4.4, a licensee is NOT required to comply with the agency disclosure requirements of Rule 4.3 when engaged in transactions with which category of party?
choice_a: First-time individual homebuyers
choice_b: Any buyer represented by an attorney
choice_c: Any seller over the age of 65
choice_d: Any corporation, non-profit corporation, professional corporation or association, LLC, partnership, REIT, business trust, charitable trust, family trust, or governmental entity
explanation: Rule 4.4 exempts licensees from the Rule 4.3 disclosure requirements when transacting with corporations, non-profit corporations, professional corporations or professional associations, LLCs, partnerships, real estate investment trusts, business trusts, charitable trusts, family trusts, or any governmental entity. The rule specifies this exception does not circumvent the underlying common law of agency.
source_note: MREC Rules and Regulations, Part 1601, Ch. 4, Rule 4.4

topic: Agency Disclosure and Duties to Parties
question: Even where the Rule 4.4 disclosure exception applies (e.g., a transaction with a corporate entity), what does the rule specifically clarify about the broker's underlying legal obligations?
choice_a: Operating under the exception does not circumvent the common law of agency
choice_b: The broker has no further duties of any kind
choice_c: The broker is automatically deemed a dual agent
choice_d: The exception eliminates fiduciary duties entirely
explanation: Rule 4.4 expressly states, 'Operating under this exception in no way circumvents the common law of agency.' The written-disclosure paperwork requirement is waived for these institutional/governmental counterparties, but the broker's substantive common-law fiduciary duties to an actual client remain intact.
source_note: MREC Rules and Regulations, Part 1601, Ch. 4, Rule 4.4

topic: Agency Disclosure and Duties to Parties
question: MREC Rule 4.2(C) defines a 'Client' as the person to whom the agent owes a fiduciary duty. Which of the following roles can a client occupy under this definition?
choice_a: Only a seller
choice_b: A seller, buyer, landlord, or tenant, or both
choice_c: Only a landlord
choice_d: Only an institutional lender
explanation: Rule 4.2(C) defines 'Client' broadly as 'the person to whom the agent owes a fiduciary duty. It can be a seller, buyer, landlord, tenant or both,' reflecting that Mississippi agency principles apply equally to sale and lease transactions.
source_note: MREC Rules and Regulations, Part 1601, Ch. 4, Rule 4.2(C)

topic: Agency Disclosure and Duties to Parties
question: MREC Rule 4.2(E) defines a 'Customer' as which of the following?
choice_a: A person who has signed a buyer representation agreement
choice_b: Any person who has paid earnest money
choice_c: A person who is not represented in a real estate transaction; it may be the buyer, seller, landlord, or tenant
choice_d: A licensee's family member
explanation: Rule 4.2(E) defines 'Customer' as 'that person not represented in a real estate transaction. It may be the buyer, seller, landlord or tenant.' A customer is owed a lesser, non-fiduciary duty of honesty and fair dealing rather than the full fiduciary duties owed to a client.
source_note: MREC Rules and Regulations, Part 1601, Ch. 4, Rule 4.2(E)

topic: Agency Disclosure and Duties to Parties
question: MREC Rule 4.2(G) enumerates the 'Fiduciary Responsibilities' owed by a Mississippi agent to a client. Which duty is described as requiring the agent to 'put the interests of the principal above the interests of the agent or any third party'?
choice_a: Obedience
choice_b: Confidentiality
choice_c: Full accounting
choice_d: Loyalty
explanation: Rule 4.2(G)(1) defines 'Loyalty' as the duty requiring the agent to 'put the interests of the principal above the interests of the agent or any third party.' Loyalty is the first of the six fiduciary duties Mississippi's rule enumerates: loyalty, obedience, disclosure, confidentiality, reasonable skill/care/diligence, and full accounting.
source_note: MREC Rules and Regulations, Part 1601, Ch. 4, Rule 4.2(G)(1)

topic: Agency Disclosure and Duties to Parties
question: Under MREC Rule 4.2(G)(4), the fiduciary duty of 'Confidentiality' requires an agent to keep private client information confidential unless the principal permits disclosure. How long does this duty continue?
choice_a: It lives on after the agency relationship is terminated
choice_b: It ends the moment the listing agreement expires
choice_c: It ends at closing
choice_d: It applies only during active negotiations
explanation: Rule 4.2(G)(4) explicitly states that the duty of confidentiality requires the agent to keep private information provided by the principal strictly confidential unless the agent has the principal's permission to disclose it, and specifically provides that 'this duty lives on after the agency relationship is terminated.' The obligation is not extinguished simply because the transaction closes or the representation ends.
source_note: MREC Rules and Regulations, Part 1601, Ch. 4, Rule 4.2(G)(4)

topic: Agency Disclosure and Duties to Parties
question: Under MREC Rule 4.2(G)(2), the fiduciary duty of 'Obedience' requires the agent to do what?
choice_a: Disclose all information the agent becomes aware of
choice_b: Obey any lawful instruction from the principal in executing the transaction that is the subject of the agency
choice_c: Provide a full accounting of funds
choice_d: Perform duties with reasonable skill and care
explanation: Rule 4.2(G)(2) defines 'Obedience' as the agent's agreement 'to obey any lawful instruction from the principal in the execution of the transaction that is the subject of the agency.' This duty is limited to lawful instructions -- an agent is not obligated (and is not permitted) to follow an unlawful directive from a client.
source_note: MREC Rules and Regulations, Part 1601, Ch. 4, Rule 4.2(G)(2)

topic: Agency Disclosure and Duties to Parties
question: Under MREC Rule 4.2(G)(6), the fiduciary duty of 'Full accounting' requires the agent to do what?
choice_a: File an annual tax return on the client's behalf
choice_b: Notify the Commission of every transaction
choice_c: Provide a full accounting of any money or goods coming into the agent's possession that belong to the principal or other parties
choice_d: Prepare a comparative market analysis
explanation: Rule 4.2(G)(6) defines 'Full accounting' as the duty to 'provide a full accounting of any money or goods coming into the agent's possession which belong to the principal or other parties' -- this duty underlies escrow/earnest-money handling requirements found elsewhere in the license law and rules.
source_note: MREC Rules and Regulations, Part 1601, Ch. 4, Rule 4.2(G)(6)

topic: Agency Disclosure and Duties to Parties
question: MREC Rule 4.1 warns that compliance with the prescribed agency disclosure form and timing rules will not always guarantee what?
choice_a: That the licensee will earn a commission
choice_b: That the transaction will close
choice_c: That continuing education credit will be awarded
choice_d: That the broker has fulfilled all responsibilities owed under the common law of agency
explanation: Rule 4.1 states that the disclosure rule 'does not abrogate the laws of agency as recognized under common law and compliance with the prescribed disclosures will not always guarantee that a Broker has fulfilled all of his responsibilities under the common law of agency.' Compliance with the paperwork protects a licensee from Commission sanctions, but it is a floor, not a ceiling, on the broker's overall duties -- especially in special situations involving vulnerable parties, where the rule advises brokers to seek legal advice before entering an agency relationship.
source_note: MREC Rules and Regulations, Part 1601, Ch. 4, Rule 4.1

topic: Agency Disclosure and Duties to Parties
question: Because a 'customer' under Mississippi's agency rule is not owed fiduciary duties such as loyalty and confidentiality, what baseline standard of conduct must a licensee nonetheless observe toward that customer?
choice_a: Honesty and fair dealing -- for example, the licensee remains subject to Section 73-35-21's prohibitions on substantial misrepresentation, false promises, and misleading advertising regardless of whether the person is a client or a customer
choice_b: No standard of conduct applies to a customer
choice_c: The licensee must still disclose all confidential client information to the customer
choice_d: The licensee must obtain the customer's written consent before speaking to them
explanation: Although a customer receives no fiduciary duties (no loyalty, obedience, or confidentiality obligations run to a customer), Mississippi licensees remain bound by baseline statutory duties of honesty and fair dealing toward everyone in a transaction. Section 73-35-21(1)(a)-(d) makes substantial misrepresentation, false promises likely to induce, a continued course of misrepresentation, and misleading advertising grounds for discipline regardless of whether the injured party was a represented client or an unrepresented customer.
source_note: Miss. Code Ann. Section 73-35-21(1)(a)-(d); MREC Rules and Regulations, Part 1601, Ch. 4, Rule 4.2(E)

topic: Agency Disclosure and Duties to Parties
question: Under MREC Rule 3.1(A), what is the responsible broker's duty with respect to the licensees sponsored under that broker?
choice_a: The broker has no supervisory duty once a license is issued
choice_b: The broker must instruct the licensees in the fundamentals of real estate practice, ethics of the profession, and the Mississippi Real Estate License Law, and must exercise supervision of their real estate activities requiring a license
choice_c: The broker's only duty is to collect commission splits
choice_d: The broker must personally attend every closing
explanation: Rule 3.1(A) makes it 'the duty of the responsible broker to instruct the licensees licensed under that broker in the fundamentals of real estate practice, ethics of the profession and the Mississippi Real Estate License Law and to exercise supervision of their real estate activities for which a license is required.' This affirmative instructional and supervisory duty is the foundation for a broker's exposure when a supervised licensee mishandles an agency disclosure.
source_note: MREC Rules and Regulations, Part 1601, Ch. 3, Rule 3.1(A)

topic: Agency Disclosure and Duties to Parties
question: Under MREC Rule 3.1(B), a real estate broker who operates under the supervision of a responsible broker (a 'broker-associate') may not act independently. To what extent is the responsible broker liable for that affiliated broker-associate's actions?
choice_a: The responsible broker has no liability because the affiliated individual is also a licensed broker
choice_b: Liability is capped at the amount of commission earned
choice_c: The responsible broker is responsible for the affiliated broker's actions to the same extent as though that licensee were a salesperson
choice_d: Liability only attaches if the responsible broker personally participated in the transaction
explanation: Rule 3.1(B) states that a broker operating under a responsible broker's supervision 'must not at any time act independently as a broker,' and that 'the responsible broker shall at all times be responsible for the action of the affiliated broker to the same extent as though that licensee were a salesperson.' The affiliated broker may not perform real estate services without the full consent and knowledge of the supervising broker.
source_note: MREC Rules and Regulations, Part 1601, Ch. 3, Rule 3.1(B)

topic: Agency Disclosure and Duties to Parties
question: Under MREC Rule 5.1(C), if a responsible broker has reason to believe that a licensee under that broker's supervision has violated the Real Estate License Law or the Commission's Rules and Regulations (for example, by failing to make a required agency disclosure), what is the broker's obligation?
choice_a: The broker may choose whether or not to report the matter
choice_b: The broker must first resolve the matter internally without ever notifying the Commission
choice_c: The broker may only report the matter if asked directly by the Commission
choice_d: It is mandatory for the responsible broker to notify the Commission
explanation: Rule 5.1(C) makes it 'mandatory for a responsible broker to notify the Commission if the responsible broker has reason to believe that a licensee for whom the broker is responsible has violated the Real Estate License Law or Rules and Regulations of the Commission.' This obligation directly implicates agency-disclosure violations committed by a broker's sponsored licensees.
source_note: MREC Rules and Regulations, Part 1601, Ch. 5, Rule 5.1(C)

topic: Agency Disclosure and Duties to Parties
question: Under MREC Rule 5.1(F), what happens to the licenses of salespersons and other licensees supervised by a responsible broker if that responsible broker's license expires, is suspended, or is revoked?
choice_a: The license of every real estate licensee currently under that broker's supervision is automatically suspended, though a licensee may then transfer to another responsible broker
choice_b: Nothing changes; supervised licensees may continue operating independently
choice_c: The supervised licensees automatically become responsible brokers themselves
choice_d: Only the licensee directly involved in the violation is suspended
explanation: Rule 5.1(F) provides that 'the expiration, suspension or revocation of a responsible broker's license shall automatically suspend the license of every real estate licensee currently under the supervision of that broker,' though the affected licensee may transfer to another responsible broker to resume active status. This underscores how deeply the supervisory relationship is embedded in every licensee's ability to operate.
source_note: MREC Rules and Regulations, Part 1601, Ch. 5, Rule 5.1(F)

topic: Agency Disclosure and Duties to Parties
question: Under MREC Rule 3.5(C), a real estate 'Team' operating within a brokerage must appoint a Team Leader who has supervisory responsibility over the team's members. What exposure does that Team Leader have if a team member under the leader's supervision violates the License Law?
choice_a: None -- only the responsible broker can be disciplined
choice_b: The Team Leader may be subject to disciplinary action for violations of the Mississippi Real Estate Brokers Act committed by team members under the leader's supervision
choice_c: The Team Leader is automatically stripped of their broker-associate license
choice_d: The Team Leader must personally refund all commissions earned by the team
explanation: Rule 3.5(C) requires every Team to appoint a Team Leader -- a broker-associate with at least one year of real estate experience -- who has supervisory responsibility (under the responsible broker) over the team's members, and expressly provides that 'the Team Leader may be subject to disciplinary action for violations of the Mississippi Real Estate Brokers Act by Team members under their supervision.'
source_note: MREC Rules and Regulations, Part 1601, Ch. 3, Rule 3.5(C)

topic: Agency Disclosure and Duties to Parties
question: Under Miss. Code Ann. Section 73-35-11 and its implementing MREC rule, when a Mississippi (resident) broker enters into a cooperative agreement allowing an out-of-state, non-Mississippi-licensed broker to cooperate on a Mississippi listing, who bears liability for the acts of that cooperating nonresident broker?
choice_a: The nonresident cooperating broker alone bears all liability
choice_b: Neither broker bears liability because the agreement is voluntary
choice_c: The Mississippi broker shall be liable for all acts of the cooperating broker, as well as for the Mississippi broker's own acts, arising from the execution of the cooperative agreement
choice_d: Liability is determined solely by which broker collected the earnest money
explanation: Section 73-35-11 provides that 'the Mississippi broker shall be liable for all acts of the above cooperating broker, as well as for his own acts, arising from the execution of any cooperative agreement.' MREC Rule 3.1(C) reinforces this, requiring the Mississippi broker to supervise showings and negotiations for in-state property and to hold earnest money in escrow. This illustrates the broad principle that Mississippi brokers bear ultimate supervisory responsibility -- including for agency-related compliance -- even for licensees or cooperating brokers they do not directly employ on a day-to-day basis.
source_note: Miss. Code Ann. Section 73-35-11; MREC Rules and Regulations, Part 1601, Ch. 3, Rule 3.1(C)
